content: To assess whether services are user-friendly, it is important to evaluate the referral process, including who makes and receives referrals and how these are conducted. This helps determine the effectiveness of networking, awareness-raising, and referral mechanisms. Follow-up services should be analyzed in terms of their frequency and the individuals involved, ensuring that all users receive appropriate follow-up care regardless of their location or the type of service unit (centralized or decentralized) they access. Repair services should be monitored to understand how often they are required, the types of repairs needed, and the reasons for them. This evaluation helps assess the technical quality of the products provided. Additionally, the frequency of prosthetic and orthotic replacements should be tracked to determine product lifespan and annual production needs. Instances of abandonment of prostheses and orthoses, along with the associated rates and reasons, should be studied to identify quality issues and areas for improvement. Understanding the primary causes of disability is essential for identifying the main types of treatment required. Monitoring these trends over time can guide service planning and predict future training needs. Data collection and analysis should be integrated into the daily operations of service units, utilizing user management systems to extract relevant statistics, preferably in graphical formats, to illustrate trends. The international prosthetics and orthotics community can support this process by developing standardized, user-friendly tools and methods for data collection at both national and international levels. Confidentiality and privacy must be respected by anonymizing data collected for statistical purposes. At the national level, stakeholders require data to monitor service delivery and plan effectively. Compiling service data into national statistics facilitates trend analysis and highlights areas needing improvement. This information can also be used to inform decision-makers and raise awareness about the achievements, challenges, and importance of prosthetics and orthotics services. Insurance companies may also find such data valuable and may invest in data collection efforts. Standardized tools and methods can streamline this process, and only data that will be utilized should be collected. A national database or register can facilitate data compilation, potentially integrating with the national health management information system. They can also support planning, monitoring, evaluation, and awareness-raising efforts. Globally, data from service and national levels can be compiled by international stakeholders to identify challenges and share examples of successful service delivery systems. Standardized evaluation criteria and ISO terminology for prosthetics and orthotics can facilitate international comparisons. Users returning for repairs or renewals can provide feedback on the utility, frequency of use, and impact of their devices on their work, education, and social participation. Systematic data collection as part of service delivery is a cost-effective way to assess impact, while more detailed impact studies may require government or stakeholder support and funding. Awareness-raising is critical, as prosthetics and orthotics services are often poorly understood, even within the health sector. Many potential beneficiaries are unaware of these services, leading to underutilization and the false impression of low demand. Awareness must be raised at all levels, from policymakers to health professionals and communities. Governments, in collaboration with national stakeholders, should promote the indispensability of these services and their benefits. Strategies should include rights-based arguments referencing national and international laws, as well as social and economic arguments highlighting cost-effectiveness and economic gains. User groups play a vital role in lobbying for policies and raising awareness. Their demands complement collected data and help decision-makers understand real-world experiences, encouraging action. Awareness-raising should also be incorporated into the training of health and social professionals and referral networks. At the grassroots level, collaboration with programs targeting similar groups, such as poverty reduction initiatives, vaccination campaigns, and disability-inclusive sports, can help raise awareness. High-quality, accessible, and affordable services naturally increase awareness among potential users, as satisfied users often share their positive experiences. International awareness-raising efforts can support national initiatives by providing adaptable guidance and resources. Information campaigns targeting the general public, decision-makers, health professionals, and potential users can be disseminated through various media, including television, radio, newspapers, social media, and schools. Role models and increased visibility of users in everyday situations, such as sports events, can also help normalize and promote these services. The image of the prosthetics and orthotics profession must be strengthened, as it is often misunderstood as merely technical or craft-based work. This perception undermines the recognition of the profession’s importance and the need for investment. National stakeholders should emphasize the extensive training and theoretical knowledge required for this field, comparable to other health and rehabilitation professions. Prosthetists and orthotists often receive university-level education, with some pursuing advanced degrees, and work closely with doctors and other health professionals. This professional image should be actively promoted. To enhance the profession’s image, prosthetics and orthotics services should be integrated into the health system, ideally within hospitals, with direct links to orthopedic, surgical, and rehabilitation departments. Positive outcomes, such as improved functionality, participation, and socioeconomic gains, should be highlighted. National recognition of the profession, including the establishment of professional associations, should be pursued. All personnel should be well-trained, use evidence-based methods, and maintain a professional appearance in service units. User areas should resemble modern hospital environments, and workshops should be clean and organized. Personnel should wear clinical uniforms and name badges, and terminology should reflect the clinical and professional nature of the work, avoiding outdated or misleading terms. Appropriate technology in prosthetics and orthotics is defined as systems that provide proper fit and alignment, meet individual needs, and are sustainable and cost-effective. Technologies should be evaluated based on user acceptability, economic feasibility, and technical suitability. Cost-effectiveness is influenced by the choice of technology, components, and materials, which should balance quality, durability, and affordability. Multiple levels of technology, from basic to advanced, may be appropriate depending on user needs and financial resources. Advanced technologies, such as microprocessor-controlled prosthetics, require higher expertise and are more expensive but may become more accessible as production processes improve. Introducing new products or methods must be accompanied by specialized training for clinical and technical personnel.
